name: Teicoplanin
route_note: IV or IM once daily after loading doses; not approved in the United States.
targets: D-alanyl-D-alanine terminus of peptidoglycan precursors (lipid II)

discovery.note: Isolated from the actinomycete Actinoplanes teichomyceticus; a lipoglycopeptide mixture of several components.

tagline: Long-acting lipoglycopeptide alternative to vancomycin, used outside the US
summary: Teicoplanin is a glycopeptide related to vancomycin, discovered by Lepetit in the 1970s. Its long half-life permits once-daily IV or IM dosing, and it is widely used in Europe for MRSA and other Gram-positive infections and for surgical prophylaxis.
mechanism: Like vancomycin, teicoplanin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of cell-wall precursors and blocks peptidoglycan polymerisation and cross-linking.

A fatty-acyl side chain anchors it to the bacterial membrane and increases plasma protein binding, prolonging its half-life. VanB-type enterococci often remain teicoplanin-susceptible because teicoplanin does not induce vanB expression, whereas VanA strains are resistant.
uses: Serious Gram-positive infections including MRSA (bacteraemia, bone and joint, skin infections)
Surgical prophylaxis in beta-lactam-allergic patients or high MRSA risk
Oral use for Clostridioides difficile infection in some countries

history.title: Glycopeptide precedent
history.detail: Vancomycin, the first glycopeptide, is approved in the US.

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Lepetit researchers in Italy describe teichomycin from Actinoplanes teichomyceticus.

history.title: VRE emerges
history.detail: Vancomycin-resistant enterococci appear in Europe; VanA strains are also teicoplanin-resistant.

history.title: Clinical launch
history.detail: Teicoplanin (Targocid) enters clinical use in Europe in the late 1980s.

history.title: Ownership
history.detail: Hoechst acquires Marion Merrell Dow, owner of Lepetit, bringing Targocid into Hoechst Marion Roussel (later Aventis).

history.title: Sanofi-Aventis
history.detail: Aventis merges with Sanofi, which continues to market Targocid.

pk.half_life: very long, about 70–100 hours or more

serious: DRESS and other severe skin reactions

facts: Teicoplanin is not approved by the US FDA despite decades of use elsewhere.
